Symbols1Summarize: The most important symbol in these verses that recurs throughout the Bible is the symbol of thirst. In this psalm, David expresses his intense longing and thirst for a relationship with God. This symbol of thirst is seen in various instances in the Bible, such as Jesus' statement "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness" (Matthew 5:6), and the invitation to come to God and drink for those who are spiritually thirsty in Isaiah 55:1. It develops throughout the Bible as a metaphor for our deep desire for God and the satisfaction that comes from finding Him.
Symbols2Summarize: The most important symbol in these verses that recurs throughout the Bible is the concept of the Lord dwelling in Zion. It signifies God's presence and protection for His people. This symbol develops throughout the Bible, as Zion becomes associated with Jerusalem and the temple, representing a physical and spiritual dwelling place for God. This motif highlights the covenant relationship between God and His people and their ultimate restoration and redemption.
Symbols3Summarize: The most important symbol in these verses that recurs throughout the Bible is the coming of the Son of Man. This symbol represents the return of Jesus Christ and the final judgment. It develops throughout the Bible with prophecies in the Old Testament (e.g. Daniel 7:13-14) and further references in the New Testament (e.g. Revelation 1:7). The coming of the Son of Man symbolizes the culmination of God's plan and the establishment of His Kingdom.
Summarize1: David expresses his deep longing and thirst for God, recognizing His power and glory. He praises and glorifies God, finding satisfaction in Him. David remembers God even in the night and finds comfort in His protection. He trusts that his enemies will be destroyed, while the king and those who trust in God will rejoice and glorify Him.
Summarize2: In Joel 3:9-21, it is proclaimed that nations should prepare for war. The Lord calls for warriors to assemble and bring down their forces. The nations are told to advance into the Valley of Jehoshaphat, where the Lord will sit in judgment. The harvest is ripe and the wickedness is great. The day of the Lord is near, and there will be darkness and trembling. The Lord will be a refuge for his people. Jerusalem will be holy and never again invaded by foreigners. Blessings will come upon God's people, with mountains dripping new wine and hills flowing with milk. Egypt and Edom will be desolate due to the violence they have done. Judah and Jerusalem will be inhabited forever. The Lord will avenge the innocent blood shed in their land.
Summarize3: In Matthew 24:29-35, Jesus describes the signs of his second coming. He says that after a time of distress, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from the sky. Then, the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven and all people on earth will mourn when they see him coming with power and glory. He will send his angels to gather his chosen ones from all over the world. Jesus also uses the analogy of a fig tree to teach that when these signs are seen, his coming is near. He assures that his words will never pass away, even though heaven and earth will.

2. The mention of the "Son of Man" and his coming on the clouds of heaven with power and glory is a reference to the return of Jesus Christ at the end times.

3. The gathering of the elect by the angels and the trumpet call can be interpreted as the final judgement and the separation of the righteous from the wicked.

5.
